content: Fairbanks disease, also known as multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED), is a rare genetic disorder that primarily affects the growth plates at the ends of bones. The dominant form of this condition occurs in approximately 1 in 10,000 live births. Normally, bones grow in length through a process where cartilage is deposited at the ends of bones, which then undergoes ossification—a process where the cartilage mineralizes and hardens into bone. In individuals with MED, this ossification process is defective. MED represents a spectrum of skeletal disorders, most of which are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. However, there is also an autosomal recessive form of the condition. Children with autosomal dominant MED often experience joint pain and fatigue following physical activity. Radiographic imaging typically reveals small and irregular ossification centers, particularly in the hips and knees. A waddling gait may develop in some cases. The spine is generally normal but may exhibit minor irregularities. By adulthood, individuals with MED are often of short stature or at the lower end of the normal height range, with disproportionately short limbs relative to their trunk. Movement at major joints, especially the elbows, may become restricted, although hypermobility can occur in the knee and finger joints. Early-onset osteoarthritis is a common complication, typically manifesting in early adulthood. Children with the recessive form of MED also experience joint pain, particularly in the hips and knees, but they are more likely to present with deformities of the hands, feet, knees, and/or vertebral column. These deformities may include scoliosis, clubfoot, cleft palate, inward-curving fingers due to underdeveloped bones, or, in rare cases, ear swelling. Prior to puberty, affected children generally have a height within the normal range. As adults, individuals with recessive MED may have a slightly reduced stature but still fall within the normal range. Functional impairments of the joints in this form are typically mild or absent.
